Lay a Trip On
LAY uh TRIP on
verb phrase (Boomer slang)
From trip, a drug experience and, by extension, any state of mind or preoccupation (mid-1960s: "a power trip," "an ego trip"), + lay on, to impose. To lay a trip on someone — to burden them with your own problems, demands, or guilt; to try to manipulate them — is late-1960s–70s counterculture slang. Its best-known descendant is guilt trip (1970s), as in "Don’t lay a guilt trip on me."

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To lay a trip on someone is to dump your expectations, problems, or guilt on them — to pressure or manipulate them emotionally. "Don’t lay that trip on me, man." Its surviving form is the guilt trip. The Christian observation: the phrase names two different things, and Scripture treats them differently. The first is manipulation — using guilt, pressure, and emotion to get one’s way. Our Lord rebuked the religious leaders who did exactly that with rules: "they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders" (Mat 23:4). A parent, a pastor, or a friend who lays guilt trips is laying burdens God never laid. The second thing the phrase can dismiss, however, is the legitimate claim of love. When a friend says "I need your help," that is not a trip; it is the law of Christ: "Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ" (Gal 6:2). The counterculture often used "don’t lay a trip on me" to refuse any obligation at all. Scripture holds both truths: bear one another’s burdens, and "every man shall bear his own burden" (Gal 6:5). And over all false guilt it speaks the gospel: "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus" (Rom 8:1); "if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart" (1Jn 3:20). The believer neither lays guilt trips nor lives under them, because the only real guilt has been carried away by the One who bore it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Late-1960s counterculture slang for burdening someone with your problems, demands, or guilt (whence guilt trip) — Scripture condemns the manipulator’s heavy burdens (Mat 23:4) but upholds bearing one another’s burdens (Gal 6:2), and frees from false guilt (Rom 8:1).

LAY A TRIP ON, v. phr. (Boomer slang, late 1960s–70s) To impose one’s own expectations, problems, or feelings on another; to pressure or manipulate, especially by inducing guilt. Hence guilt trip (1970s); ego trip, power trip.

Webster (1828) — LAY, verb transitive 15. To asses; to charge; to impose; as, to lay a tax on land; to lay a duty on salt. 16. To charge; to impute; as, to lay blame on one; to lay want of prudence to one’s charge. 17. To impose, as evil, burden, or punishment. The Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all. Isaiah 5:6 3.

Decode for families: "Mom, you’re guilt-tripping me" is this phrase in its Gen Z form.

Key Scripture

Mat 23:4 — "For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers."

Gal 6:2 — "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ."

Gal 6:5 — "For every man shall bear his own burden."

Rom 8:1 — "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit."

1Jn 3:20 — "For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things."

Modern Corruption

The phrase rightly resists emotional manipulation but was often used to refuse any obligation of love; Scripture forbids laying false burdens, commands bearing one another’s burdens, and lifts false guilt in Christ.

expand to see more

Every family knows the guilt trip: the sigh, the reminder of all that has been sacrificed, the hint that a good son would call more often. It is a sin, because it uses love as a lever, and it usually fails, because guilt produces resentment rather than love. Our Lord saw it in its religious form — burdens laid on the people by men who would not lift a finger (Mat 23:4) — and He offered instead an easy yoke.

But the 1960s turned the phrase into a shield against every claim. A parent’s request, a friend’s need, a church’s call to duty — all could be dismissed as someone "laying a trip." Galatians 6 refuses that dismissal: bearing burdens is the law of Christ (Gal 6:2). The difference between a burden of love and a guilt trip is whether it is offered freely or extracted by pressure. A Christian family learns to ask freely, give gladly, and leave guilt where Christ left it — nailed to the cross (Rom 8:1).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Lay on (to impose) + mid-1960s trip (a state of mind) → late-1960s lay a trip on → 1970s guilt trip, ego trip, power trip.

expand to see more

Old English lecgan — to lay, to place; lay on — to impose (a burden, a tax)

Mid-1960s: trip — a drug experience; then any mental state or preoccupation

Late 1960s: lay a trip on — to burden or manipulate

1970s: guilt trip; ego trip; power trip

Greek baros — a burden borne for another (Gal 6:2); phortion — one’s own load (Gal 6:5)

Usage

""Grandma never laid a guilt trip on anyone. She just made pie and waited.""

"Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ (Gal 6:2)."

"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1)."
